A recent Stat 272 project examined determinants of covid vaccination rates at the county level.  Our data set contains 3053 rows (1 for each county in the US) and 14 columns; here is a quick description of the variables we'll be using:

- `state` = state the county is located in
- `county` = name of the county
- `region` = region the state is located in
- `metro_status` = Is the county considered "Metro" or "Non-metro"?
- `rural_urban_code` = from 1 (most urban) to 9 (most rural)
- `perc_complete_vac` = percent of county completely vaccinated as of 11/9/21
- `tot_pop` = total population in the county
- `votes_Trump` = number of votes for Trump in the county in 2020
- `votes_Biden` = number of votes for Biden in the county in 2020
- `perc_Biden` = percent of votes for Biden in the county in 2020
- `ed_somecol_perc` = percent with some education beyond high school (but not a Bachelor's degree)
- `ed_bachormore_perc` = percent with a Bachelor's degree or more
- `unemployment_rate_2020` = county unemployment rate in 2020
- `median_HHincome_2019` = county's median household income in 2019


1. Consider only Minnesota and its surrounding states (Iowa, Wisconsin, North Dakota, and South Dakota).  We want to examine the relationship between the percentage who voted for Biden and the percentage of complete vaccinations by state.  Generate two plots to examine this relationship:

a) A scatterplot with points and smoothers colored by state.  Make sure the legend is ordered in a meaningful way, and include good labels on your axes and your legend.  Also leave off the error bars from your smoothers.

```{r}
vaccine_data |>
  filter(state %in% c("Minnesota","Wisconsin","Iowa","North Dakota","South Dakota")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = perc_Biden, y = perc_complete_vac, color = fct_reorder2(state, perc_Biden, perc_complete_vac))) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Percent of population who voted for Biden",
       y = "Percentage of complete vaccination",
       title = "Relationship between voting for Biden and Vaccination Status",
       color = "State")
```


b) One plot per state containing a scatterplot and a smoother.

```{r}
vaccine_data |>
  filter(state %in% c("Minnesota","Wisconsin","Iowa","North Dakota","South Dakota")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = perc_Biden, y = perc_complete_vac, color = state)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~state)
  labs(x = "Percent of population who voted for Biden",
       y = "Percentage of complete vaccination",
       title = "Relationship between voting for Biden and Vaccination Status",
       color = "State")
```

Describe which plot you prefer and why.  What can you learn from your preferred plot?

I prefer the second one because the first one is very messy and busy. It's a little more difficult to make out trends in the first plot compared to the second plot.

2. We wish to compare the proportions of counties in each region with median household income above the national median ($69,560).

a) Fill in the blanks below to produce a segmented bar plot with regions ordered from highest proportion above the median to lowest.

b) Create a table of proportions by region to illustrate that your bar plot in (a) is in the correct order (you should find two regions that are *really* close when you just try to eyeball differences).

c) Explain why we can replace `fct_relevel(region, FILL IN CODE)` with

`mutate(region_sort = fct_reorder(region, median_HHincome_2019 < 69560, .fun = mean))` 

but not

`mutate(region_sort = fct_reorder(region, median_HHincome_2019 < 69560))`

```{r}
#| eval: false

vaccine_data |>
  mutate(HHincome_vs_national = ifelse(median_HHincome_2019 < 69560, FILL IN CODE)) |>
  mutate(region_sort = fct_relevel(region, FILL IN CODE)) |>
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = region_sort, fill = HHincome_vs_national)) +
    geom_bar(position = "fill")
```

4. Produce 3 different plots for illustrating the relationship between the rural_urban_code and percent vaccinated.  Hint: you can sometimes turn numeric variables into categorical variables for plotting purposes (e.g. `as.factor()`, `ifelse()`).

```{r}
vaccine_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = as.factor(rural_urban_code), y = perc_complete_vac, fill = as.factor(rural_urban_code) )) +
  geom_boxplot()

vaccine_data |>
  mutate(majority_vaccinated = ifelse(perc_complete_vac < 50, "No", "Yes")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = majority_vaccinated, y = rural_urban_code, fill = majority_vaccinated)) +
  geom_boxplot()

vaccine_data |>
  mutate(majority_vaccinated = ifelse(perc_complete_vac < 50, "No", "Yes")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = as.factor(rural_urban_code), fill = majority_vaccinated)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill")

```

State your favorite plot, why you like it better than the other two, and what you can learn from your favorite plot.  Create an alt text description of your favorite plot, using the Four Ingredient Model.  See [this link](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1BuEbL6vETBcFULmtlrwwZBUYhdEg0Zqb/view?usp=sharing) for reminders and references about alt text.

My favorite plot is the first plot. This is because I think it is the easiest to comprehend and it's visually the most appealing. From this box plot, we can see a general trend that the more rural a county is, the less likely it is for the inhabitants of that county are to be vaccinated.

This plot depicts a boxplot showing the relationship between the rural/urban code of a county, and the percentage of the inhabitants of those counties that are completely vaccinated. On the x-axis is the rural/urban codes, which range from 1 (most urban) to 9 (most rural), and there is a boxplot for each of these 9 codes. On the y-axis is the percent of each county that is completely vaccinated, which ranges from about 0% vaccinated to about 85% vaccinated. The general trend that we can spot from the plot is that the more rural a county is, the less vaccinated that county is likely to be. So the most urban counties (with a code of 1) are the most vaccinated, as their average percentage that is completely vaccinated is a little over 50%. Meanwhile, the most rural counties (with a code of 9) have an average percentage that is completely vaccinated that is about 40%.


5. BEFORE running the code below, sketch the plot that will be produced by R.  AFTER running the code, describe what conclusion(s) can we draw from this plot?  

This plot shows the voting variation among the ten states with the most counties. States towards the bottom of the y axis had most of its counties not vote for Biden, suggesting that these are stronger Republican states. Meanwhile, states toward the top of the y axis are more of a mixed bag; there are some counties in these states that voted very strongly for Biden, while other counties in the state voted very strongly against Biden. These kind of states might be more purple/battleground states.

```{r}
#| eval: FALSE

vaccine_data |>
  filter(!is.na(perc_Biden)) |> #filter out NA rows in the perc-Biden variable
  mutate(big_states = fct_lump(state, n = 10)) |> #Lumps the states by collecting the 10 states with the most counties in the dataset, and then all other states are lumped into "other"
  group_by(big_states) |> #Group by the 10 most frequent states in the dataset
  summarize(IQR_Biden = IQR(perc_Biden)) |> #Finds the interquartile range for each of the grouped by states
  mutate(big_states = fct_reorder(big_states, IQR_Biden)) |> #Order the states based so that the smallest IQR is at the bottom of the y axis, and the state with the largest IQR is at the top of the y axis
  ggplot() + 
    geom_point(aes(x = IQR_Biden, y = big_states)) #Creates a scatterplot with IQR on the x axis and the states on the y axis
```


6. In this question we will focus only on the 12 states in the Midwest (i.e. where region == "Midwest").

a) Create a tibble with the following information for each state.  Order states from least to greatest state population.

- number of different `rural_urban_code`s represented among the state's counties (there are 9 possible)
- total state population
- proportion of Metro counties
- median unemployment rate 

```{r}
midwest_vacc <- vaccine_data |>
  filter(region == "Midwest")

midwest_tib <- midwest_vacc |>
  group_by(state) |>
  summarize(
    num_codes = n_distinct(rural_urban_code),
    state_pop = sum(tot_pop),
    prop_metro = mean(metro_status == "Metro"),
    median_unemp = median(unemployment_rate_2020)
  ) |>
  arrange(state_pop)

midwest_tib
```


b) Use your tibble in (a) to produce a plot of the relationship between proportion of Metro counties and median unemployment rate.  Points should be colored by the number of different `rural_urban_code`s in a state, but a single linear trend should be fit to all points.  What can you conclude from the plot?

From the plot, we can conclude that a higher proportion of metro counties in a state is associated with a higher median unemployment rate in the state. There doesn't appear to be a super clear trend with number of different rural/urban codes, but we can roughly see a slight association that for the more unique rural/urban codes a state has, the higher the median unemployment rate.

```{r}
midwest_tib |>
  ggplot(aes(x = prop_metro, y = median_unemp)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = num_codes)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "black") +
  labs(x = "Proportion of Metro Counties",
       y = "Median Unemployment Rate",
       title = "Relationship between Porportion of Metor Counties and Median Unemployment Rate",
       color = "Number of different Rural/Urban Codes")
```

In this next section, we consider a few variables that could have been included in our data set, but were NOT.  Thus, you won't be able to write and test code, but you nevertheless should be able to use your knowledge of the tidyverse to answer these questions.

Here are the hypothetical variables:

- HR_party = party of that county's US Representative (Republican, Democrat, Independent, Green, or Libertarian)
- people_per_MD = number of residents per doctor (higher values = fewer doctors)
- perc_over_65 = percent of residents over 65 years old
- perc_white = percent of residents who identify as white


8. Hypothetical R chunk #1:

```{r}
#| eval: false

# Hypothetical R chunk 1
temp <- vaccine_data |>
  mutate(new_perc_vac = ifelse(perc_complete_vac > 95, NA, perc_complete_vac),
         MD_group = cut_number(people_per_MD, 3)) |>
  group_by(MD_group) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_perc_vac = mean(new_perc_vac, na.rm = TRUE),
            mean_white = mean(perc_white, na.rm = TRUE))
```  

a) Describe the tibble `temp` created above.  What would be the dimensions?  What do rows and columns represent?

The tibble created above would have 3 rows, since `cut_number` creates 3 groups, and 4 columns. The 4 columns would be MD_group, n, mean_perc_vac, and mean_white. Each row represent one of the 3 groups we created from people_per_MD. The first column, MD_group, identifies each group we created, then the n column tells us how many people are in each group, the mean_perc_vac column tells us the mean percentage vaccinated for each group, and mean_white tells us the mean percentage of white people for each group.

b) What would happen if we replaced `new_perc_vac = ifelse(perc_complete_vac > 95, NA, perc_complete_vac)` with `new_perc_vac = ifelse(perc_complete_vac > 95, perc_complete_vac, NA)`?

If we replaced `new_perc_vac = ifelse(perc_complete_vac > 95, NA, perc_complete_vac)` with `new_perc_vac = ifelse(perc_complete_vac > 95, perc_complete_vac, NA)`, then instead of replacing the perc_complete_vac of all the counties with a perc_complete_vac > 95 with an NA, we would replace the perc_complete_vac of every county with a perc_complete_vac < 95 with an NA.

c) What would happen if we replaced `mean_white = mean(perc_white, na.rm = TRUE)` with `mean_white = mean(perc_white)`?

If we replaced `mean_white = mean(perc_white, na.rm = TRUE)` with `mean_white = mean(perc_white)`, NA will be returned as the mean_white value for a group if there are any NA values under the perc_white column for any of the observational units in a group.

d) What would happen if we removed `group_by(MD_group)`?

If we removed `group_by(MD_group)`, we would no longer have summary data for three groups. Instead, we would have n, mean_perc_vac, and mean_white for the whole dataset.

9. Hypothetical R chunk #2:

```{r}
#| eval: false

# Hypothetical R chunk 2
ggplot(data = vaccine_data) +
  geom_point(mapping = aes(x = perc_over_65, y = perc_complete_vac, 
                           color = HR_party)) +
  geom_smooth()

temp <- vaccine_data |>
  group_by(HR_party) |>
  summarise(var1 = n()) |>
  arrange(desc(var1)) |>
  slice_head(n = 3)

vaccine_data |>
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = fct_reorder(HR_party, perc_over_65, .fun = median), 
                       y = perc_over_65)) +
    geom_boxplot()
```

a) Why would the first plot produce an error?

The first plot produces an error because there are no aesthetic mappings supplied in the geom_smooth layer of the plot. Only the geom_point layer of the plot has aesthetic mappings supplied.
 
b) Describe the tibble `temp` created above.  What would be the dimensions?  What do rows and columns represent?

The tibble created above would have 3 rows and 2 columns. There would be 3 rows because `slice_head(n = 3)` takes the top 3 rows, and there are 2 columns, which would be HR_party and var1. The HR_party column comes from grouping by HR_party, and the var1 column comes from `summarise(var1 = n())`. Additionally, the 3 rows selected would have the 3 most common values for HR_party among the whole dataset, because of the line `arrange(desc(var1))`.

c) What would happen if we replaced `fct_reorder(HR_party, perc_over_65, .fun = median)` with `HR_party`?

The order that the HR_party variable is displayed on the plot would change. Without `fct_reorder`, HR_party will be plotted in the order it appears in the dataset, rather than the median value of each group's perc_over_65 value.

10. Hypothetical R chunk #3:

```{r}
#| eval: false

# Hypothetical R chunk 3
vaccine_data |>
  filter(!is.na(people_per_MD)) |>
  mutate(state_lump = fct_lump(state, n = 4)) |>
  group_by(state_lump, rural_urban_code) |>
  summarise(mean_people_per_MD = mean(people_per_MD)) |>
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = rural_urban_code, y = mean_people_per_MD, 
      colour = fct_reorder2(state_lump, rural_urban_code, mean_people_per_MD))) +
    geom_line()
```

a) Describe the tibble piped into the ggplot above.  What would be the dimensions?  What do rows and columns represent?

This tibble has 45 rows and 3 columns. There are 45 rows because we're grouping by state_lump and rural_urban_code. This means that we're taking the 4 states with the most counties, and grouping together the counties with the same rural_urban_code in each of these 4 states. And then all other counties in the dataset are lumped together based on their rural_urban_code. The total number of rows in the dataset can be represented by $5 \times 9$, since we have 4 states + other = 5, and then 9 codes for each of these 5 groups. There are 3 columns, which are state, rural_urban_code, and mean_people_per_MD. 

b) Carefully describe the plot created above.

On the x-axis of the plot would be the variable rural_urban_code, which ranges from 1 to 9. Then, on the y-axis would be mean_people_per_MD. Then, there's a line to represent each state, and the color of each line is matches up with the legend so that the state that has the largest mean_people_per_MD with an area code of 9 is at the top of the legend, and the state with the smallest mean_people_per_MD with an area code of 9 is at the bottom of the legend.

c) What would happen if we removed `filter(!is.na(people_per_MD))`?

If we removed `filter(!is.na(people_per_MD))`, then mean_people_per_MD would show NA for any of the groups that have a row with NA for the people_per_MD variable.

d) What would happen if we replaced `fct_reorder2(state_lump, rural_urban_code, mean_people_per_MD)` with `state_lump`?

If we replaced `fct_reorder2(state_lump, rural_urban_code, mean_people_per_MD)` with `state_lump`, then the plot would be more difficult to read. The order of the states in the legned wouldn't match up with the order of each state's line on the plot when rural_urban_code = 9.
